title: Desert Animals
keyIdea: A desert is a habitat with very little rain or snow, under about 250 mm a year. Deserts can be hot or cold, but they are always dry. Desert animals have adaptations for heat and little water: a fennec fox's big ears let heat out, meerkats dig cool burrows, a camel's hump stores fat (not water) and it drinks a lot at once, a kangaroo rat gets water from its food, and scorpions hide by day and hunt at night.
familyTip: Next time it is hot outside, test the shade idea together. Put one hand on a sunny path and one on soil in the shade, or under a stone. Which is cooler? Ask your child which desert animal uses that trick, and why a burrow under the sand stays cool.

visual.caption: Does each trick help with heat, or with finding and saving water? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

items: scorpion: hides under rocks by day

lab.caption: Flagship lab: measure rain in five places, grow a fennec fox's ears, dig a meerkat to its nest, fill a camel's hump, match tricks.

kid: A desert is a place with very little rain or snow. The Sahara is a hot desert. The Gobi has freezing winters. The middle of Antarctica is a cold desert too. Hot or cold, a desert is always dry.
Desert animals have special ways to cope. We call these adaptations. The fennec fox has huge thin ears. Heat from its warm blood leaves through them, so the fox stays cool.
Meerkats dig burrows. The sand on top can burn in the sun, but deep down the soil stays cool. Scorpions and rattlesnakes hide in the shade by day and come out when it is cooler.

Many people think a camel's hump holds water. It does not. It is a store of fat. A camel can go days without a drink, then gulp a huge amount at once. A kangaroo rat may never drink: it gets water from the seeds it eats.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This fits the National Curriculum in England for Year 2, living things and their habitats. Pupils learn how a habitat meets the basic needs of the animals in it. It leads into Year 4 (environments can change) and Year 6 (animals are adapted to suit their environment in different ways). Key words: habitat, adaptation, nocturnal, burrow, predator and prey.

A desert is defined by low rain and snow, often under about 250 mm a year. Heat and sand are not part of the test. The centre of the Sahara gets under about 25 mm, the Gobi about 190 mm, and inland Antarctica about 50 mm. Fennec fox ears can be about 15 cm long. They have many blood vessels that give off heat, and they hear prey under the sand. Meerkat burrows stay far cooler than the surface sand, which can pass 60 °C on a summer afternoon. A camel's hump is fat. Camels lose little water, and a thirsty camel can drink about 135 litres in around 13 minutes. Kangaroo rats get almost all their water from seeds and from breaking down food. Many desert animals are nocturnal.

Common mistakes: thinking all deserts are hot and sandy; believing the camel's hump stores water; saying big ears keep a fox warm (small ears keep heat in, as in the Arctic fox); thinking some animals need no water at all, when they get it from food; and guessing that burrows are hotter because they are closed in.

In the lab your child taps rain gauges for five places against a 250 mm line. They drag a fennec fox's ears bigger until a heat bar turns green. They drag a meerkat down a tunnel past a thermometer, from 65 °C to about 30 °C. They drag fat, not water, into a camel's hump and let it drink 135 litres. Last, they match five animals to their tricks. The temperatures are a typical example, not fixed values.

practice.prompt: What makes a place a desert?
choices: it gets very little rain or snow
practice.hint: Think of Antarctica. It is icy, not hot or sandy, but it is still a desert.
practice.explain: A desert gets very little rain or snow, under about 250 mm a year. Some deserts are cold and many are rocky, not sandy.

practice.prompt: What is stored in a camel's hump?
practice.hint: The camel can use what is in the hump for energy when food is short.
practice.explain: The hump is fat. Camels save water in other ways and can drink a huge amount at once.

practice.prompt: A desert got {a} mm of rain one year and {b} mm the next. How much rain fell in the two years altogether?
practice.hint: Add the two years together: {a} + {b}. Both are small numbers for rain.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} mm. That is still very little rain for two whole years.

practice.prompt: The sand on top is {t} °C. Deep in a meerkat's burrow it is 30 °C. How many degrees cooler is the burrow?
practice.hint: Find the difference: take 30 away from {t}.
practice.explain: {t} − 30 = {=t-30}. The burrow is {=t-30} °C cooler, because the soil above blocks the sun.

practice.prompt: Why does a fennec fox have such big ears?
choices: to let body heat escape and to hear prey
to keep its head warm at night
practice.hint: Warm blood flows through the thin skin of the ears. What happens to the heat?
practice.explain: Big thin ears let heat leave the body, and they help the fox hear insects under the sand. Small ears keep heat in, like an Arctic fox's.

pool.prompt: The Gobi Desert has freezing winters. Why is it still a desert?
choices: it gets very little rain or snow
it is a desert only in summer
pool.hint: A desert is about how much rain or snow falls, not how hot it is.
pool.explain: The Gobi gets about 190 mm of rain and snow a year, under the 250 mm mark, so it is a cold desert.

pool.prompt: At midday, why do meerkats go down into their burrows?
choices: deep soil is cooler than the sand on top
pool.hint: The soil above the burrow blocks the sun.
pool.explain: Surface sand can get hot enough to burn, but deep soil stays much cooler, so the burrow is a safe place in the heat.

pool.prompt: How does a kangaroo rat get water if it hardly ever drinks?
choices: it needs no water at all
pool.hint: Every animal needs water. Where else could water come from?
pool.explain: It gets water from its food: seeds, and water made when its body breaks the food down. It also loses very little.

pool.prompt: A thirsty camel drinks {n} litres in one go. A bath holds about 80 litres. How many litres more than a bath is that?
pool.hint: Take 80 away from {n} to compare the two amounts.
pool.explain: {n} − 80 = {=n-80} litres more than a bath. Camels drink a lot at once and then can go days without water.

pool.prompt: Which animal is NOT a desert animal?
pool.hint: Two of these live in hot, dry places. One lives on Arctic sea ice.
pool.explain: Polar bears live on Arctic sea ice. Fennec foxes live in the Sahara and meerkats in the Kalahari.

pool.prompt: Scorpions hide under rocks in the day. When do they usually hunt?
choices: at night, when it is cooler
pool.hint: Hiding by day keeps them out of the hottest sun.
pool.explain: Many desert animals, like scorpions, are nocturnal: they rest in shade by day and hunt in the cooler night.

pool.prompt: Ali says big ears keep a fennec fox warm. What is the mistake?
choices: big ears let heat out, so they keep the fox cool
pool.hint: Compare the Arctic fox, which lives in the cold and has small ears.
pool.explain: Big thin ears lose heat, which helps in the hot desert. Small ears, like an Arctic fox's, keep heat in.

pool.prompt: A desert gets {r} mm of rain a year. The desert mark is 250 mm. How many mm under the mark is it?
pool.hint: Find the difference between 250 and {r} by taking {r} away from 250.
pool.explain: 250 − {r} = {=250-r} mm under the mark, so it is dry enough to be a desert.
